strengths: The paper tackles an important and relevant problem: bridging theoretical learnability guarantees for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection with modern transformer architectures.
The empirical evaluation covers multiple modalities and model types, including vision (ViT-B-16) and language tasks across encoder-only (BERT) and decoder-only (GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B) backbones.
The proposed GROD framework provides a comprehensive pipeline for feature-space outlier generation combining PCA/LDA boundary search, Mahalanobis-based filtering, and soft-label regularization.
weaknesses: Mathematical soundness in the theoretical analysis is severely flawed. In Definition 4.4, the 'probability of OOD detection learnability' is defined via the Lebesgue measure $\mu$ of sets of distributions $\mathcal{D}_{XY}^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, which is mathematically ill-defined because distributions and spaces of distributions are not subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Flawed probabilistic step in the proofs of Lemma C.5 and Theorems 4.5/4.6: The derivation in Eq. (42) and Lemma C.5 appears to treat the representation of multiple discrete hypotheses $h_1, \dots, h_\delta$ as independent events, multiplying probabilities together and raising $(1 - \dots)$ to the power of $(K+1)\delta$. Universal representation of a hypothesis space is an intersection of representation events, not a product of independent trials; raising this probability to an exponential power is theoretically unfounded.

Trivialized setting of finite input space: Theorem 4.3 requires $|\mathcal{X}| < +\infty$ for learnability in the separate space, directly inheriting the impossibility results of Fang et al. (2022). Restricting the analysis to a finite domain $|\mathcal{X}| < \infty$ trivializes the statistical PAC learning problem, as any sufficiently expressive model can simply memorize a finite set of points.

Loose connection between theory and algorithm: The theoretical results merely reiterate that misclassifying OOD as ID must be penalized (a direct restatement of the condition $l(y_2, y_1) \le l(K+1, y_1)$ from Fang et al., 2022) and that model capacity matters. The specific heuristics of GROD—such as 1D PCA/LDA boundary extraction, Mahalanobis distance filtering, and autoregressive mean tracking—are ad-hoc and not derived from or guided by the formal theory.

Presentation and writing issues: Several typographical errors are present throughout the text and section headings, such as 'Abaltion study' (pages 28 and 29), 'We do not exam' (page 4), and 'the letter develops' (Remark B.3). Furthermore, on page 23, the sentence 'The code is publicly available at' is left unfinished with no link provided.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely topic: understanding the theoretical capabilities and limits of transformer architectures for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and using these insights to motivate better algorithms.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning both computer vision (ViT-B-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200) and natural language processing tasks (BERT, GPT-2, and LLaMA-3.1-8B on IMDB/Yelp and CLINC150), showing competitive performance across multiple benchmarks.
Comprehensive appendix providing detailed ablation studies on hyper-parameters, visualization of synthetic feature distributions via t-SNE, and likelihood distribution plots.
weaknesses: Mathematical and conceptual flaws in the theoretical foundation: Definition 4.4 ('Probability of the OOD detection learnability') is mathematically ill-posed. Equation (9) takes the ratio of Lebesgue measures mu(D'_{XY}) / mu(D_{XY}) in R^d, but D_{XY} is defined as a space of probability distributions (or a distribution), which is not a subset of Euclidean space endowed with standard Lebesgue measure.

Flawed transition from Jackson-type approximation to classifier PAC learnability: In the proofs of Lemma C.2 and Lemma C.5, the authors apply Chebyshev/Markov inequalities to an L1/L2 integral approximation bound over the input domain, yielding a probability bound under the input distribution's Lebesgue measure. However, classifying discrete labels via argmax requires uniform (L_infinity) error control or pointwise bounds across all sample points; showing that an L1 integral is small does not guarantee that argmax_k f^k(x) = h(x) uniformly or with high probability across arbitrary distributions.

Limited theoretical novelty beyond existing work: Lemma 4.1 trivially embeds FCNNs into transformers by zeroing out self-attention weights. Theorem 4.3 essentially substitutes the FCNN universal approximation property (UAP) in the proof template of Fang et al. (2022) with known transformer UAP results (Yun et al., 2019; Jiang & Li, 2023).

Disconnect between theoretical results and the proposed GROD algorithm: While the paper claims GROD is derived from the theory, the theorems merely demonstrate the well-known requirement that the training loss must penalize OOD errors (Fang et al., 2022). The specific empirical components of GROD—such as PCA/LDA boundary point extraction, heuristic Gaussian extension, Mahalanobis distance filtering, and soft labeling—are heuristic feature-space synthesis techniques without direct theoretical backing from the Jackson bounds.

Presentation and readability issues in the main body: Algorithm 1 on page 6 directly cites Equations (51) through (68), none of which exist in the main paper—they only appear in Appendix E (pages 21–23). A paper's core algorithm must be fully defined and self-contained within the main text.

Conflation of fine-tuning gains and post-processing: GROD couples synthetic outlier fine-tuning with a modified VIM post-processor at test time (Section 6, Eq. 68). Because VIM alone already achieves very strong baseline results (e.g., Table 1), it is difficult to cleanly isolate how much performance gain comes from the proposed synthetic outliers versus the choice and tuning of the post-processor.

strengths: Ambitious objective: Attempting to establish a formal theoretical foundation for Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection specifically tailored to transformer architectures is a timely and important research direction.

Broad empirical evaluation: The empirical component includes evaluations across both computer vision (ViT) and natural language processing tasks (BERT, GPT-2, and Llama-3.1-8B) on several standard benchmark datasets.

Algorithmic design: The proposed GROD method introduces an intuitive geometric approach for generating synthetic outliers in the feature space by combining PCA and LDA boundary projections with Mahalanobis-based filtering.
weaknesses: Severe mathematical and conceptual flaws in the theoretical foundations: The formulation of 'probability of OOD detection learnability' (Definition 4.4, Theorems 4.5 and 4.6) is mathematically unsound. Eq. (9) takes the Lebesgue measure of a distribution / distribution space, which is ill-defined. Furthermore, the proofs of Lemma C.2, Lemma C.5, and Theorem C.1 apply Markov's inequality (erroneously referred to as Chebyshev's inequality in Eq. (30)) over the spatial domain $x \in I$ from an $L_1$ Jackson-type approximation bound, and then conflate this spatial error measure with the probability that a deterministic hypothesis belongs to a deterministic hypothesis space $\mathcal{H}^{(m,2)}$. A spatial approximation guarantee on $x$ does not imply PAC learnability probability across datasets.

Derivative theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.3 relies almost entirely on the proof architecture of Theorem 10 in Fang et al. (2022), simply substituting the FCNN universal approximation property with known transformer approximation results (Yun et al., 2019; Jiang & Li, 2023) or embedding FCNNs into transformers via zeroed self-attention weights (Lemma 4.1). The resulting necessary and sufficient condition ($|\mathcal{X}| < +\infty$) is a direct inheritance from Fang et al. (2022) rather than an intrinsic insight into self-attention or transformer dynamics.

Disconnect between theoretical claims and the GROD algorithm: The paper asserts that GROD is derived from the theoretical framework. However, the theoretical theorems only state existence and PAC learnability under idealized separation and label penalties. The specific pipeline in GROD—PCA/LDA boundary search, autoregressive center updating, Gaussian perturbation, Mahalanobis filtering, and VIM post-processing—is an empirical heuristic following prior virtual outlier synthesis literature (e.g., VOS, NPOS) rather than a mathematically derived consequence of Theorems 4.3–4.6.

Inconsistencies and imprecise presentation: The manuscript contains multiple notation collisions and drafting errors (e.g., Chebyshev's vs. Markov's inequality in Section C; undefined notations such as $\mathcal{H}_{tood}^{(m,l)}$ appearing abruptly in Theorem C.1; missing references and unfinished descriptions in Section C/D; broken references such as 'Lemmas 1316 in Fang et al. (2022)').

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving out-of-distribution (OOD) detection capabilities in transformer architectures.
The empirical evaluation spans both vision (ViT) and natural language processing (BERT) across several benchmarks, comparing against multiple post-processing and fine-tuning baselines.
The authors conduct ablation studies exploring the sensitivity of key hyperparameters ($\gamma, \alpha, num$) and the impact of individual pipeline components.
weaknesses: Theoretical formulations contain severe mathematical flaws and vacuous settings: (1) In Theorem 1 / Theorem 4, learnability is stated to hold 'if and only if $|\mathcal{X}| = n < +\infty$'. Restricting the input domain $\mathcal{X}$ to be finite reduces the problem to trivial finite-sample memorization, bypassing the core challenge of continuous distribution-free OOD PAC learnability identified by Fang et al. (2022). (2) Definition 5 defines the probability of learnability via the ratio of Lebesgue measures $\mu(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{'n}) / \mu(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^n)$, where $\mu$ is stated to be 'the Lebesgue measure in $\mathbb{R}^d$'. Distributions are probability measures over sample spaces, not subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$; taking the Lebesgue measure of a set of distributions is mathematically ill-defined.

Methodological inconsistency in projection inversion: In Section 3, Eq. (3), boundary points obtained in the projected spaces $\mathbb{R}^{num}$ ($num \le d$, set to $1$ in practice) are mapped back to the feature space $\mathbb{R}^d$ using $\text{PCA}^{-1}$ and $\text{LDA}^{-1}$, described as 'inverse mappings according to set theory'. Dimensionality reduction projections are non-injective; their set-theoretic pre-images are $(d - num)$-dimensional affine subspaces, not discrete vectors. The manuscript does not specify how unique reconstruction vectors are determined.

Experimental anomalies and lack of rigor: In Table 2, GROD reports an FPR@95 of 0.16% on CIFAR-10 vs CIFAR-100 without real outlier exposure. This near-zero error is anomalous for CIFAR-10 vs CIFAR-100 near-OOD detection, especially when inverted in Table 3 (CIFAR-100 as ID, CIFAR-10 as OOD), where GROD achieves an FPR@95 of 43.38%. Furthermore, in Table 6, ablating any single component leaves FPR@95 around 9.85%–13.46%, yet combining all three causes an abrupt plunge to 0.12%. Such drastic discontinuities require thorough explanation and verification.

Significant presentation and formatting issues: (1) The abstract ends with an unfinished sentence: 'The code is available a'. (2) Multiple broken internal references in Section 4 (referencing non-existent 'Table 4.2' and 'Table 4.3' instead of Table 5 and Table 6). (3) Broken citation rendering in Appendix E ('Lemmas 1316 in ~ Fang et al. (2022)'). (4) Frequent typos throughout (e.g., 'scAtter', 'correspongding', 'analysized').

strengths: The paper addresses an important and active research problem: improving out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance in transformer architectures across vision and language modalities.
The empirical evaluation spans both computer vision (ViT on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200) and natural language processing (BERT on CLINC150 and IMDB/Yelp), which provides cross-modal coverage.

The inclusion of ablation studies examining the loss weighting parameter $\gamma$, distance factor $\alpha$, outlier cluster count $num$, and individual algorithmic components provides useful analysis of the method's mechanics.
weaknesses: Severe mathematical and conceptual issues in the theoretical formulation: Definition 5 attempts to define the probability of learnability via a ratio of Lebesgue measures $\mu(D_{XY}^{'n}) / \mu(D_{XY}^n)$ using 'the Lebesgue measure in $\mathbb{R}^d$', which is mathematically ill-posed because distributions are probability measures on function/sample spaces, not subsets of finite Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$. Furthermore, the bound in Theorem 2/5 scales as $(1 - \dots)^{(K+1)n+1}$, which decays exponentially toward zero as sample size $n$ grows, contradicting standard learning-theoretic guarantees where larger sample sizes improve bounds.

Trivialization of the transformer architecture in theoretical proofs: In Lemma 1, the expressivity proof explicitly sets the attention projection matrix $W_O^i = 0$, thereby zeroing out the self-attention mechanism completely and treating the transformer purely as a feed-forward network. Consequently, the theoretical guarantees do not reflect self-attention dynamics or sequence representations.

Ill-defined algorithmic steps: In Eq. (2) and Eq. (3), boundary points obtained from LDA projections ($num \le d$) are mapped back to the feature space via '$\text{LDA}^{-1}$ according to set theory'. LDA is a non-invertible dimensionality reduction mapping whose preimage is an affine subspace rather than a single feature vector; the paper does not explain how a unique point is reconstructed.

Scalability limitation inherent to the LDA formulation: Because LDA requires multiple samples per class within each mini-batch (Eq. 4-5), the inter-class outlier synthesis fails when the number of classes exceeds batch capacity. Consequently, the authors are forced to set $|I|=0$ (disabling LDA) for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-200, where GROD achieves only incremental or inferior results compared to existing methods like CIDER and NPOS (e.g., CIDER outperforms GROD on CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 OOD detection in Table 4).

Incomplete writing and poor presentation quality: The abstract cuts off mid-sentence ('The code is available a'), Section 1 cuts off abruptly at the bottom of page 1 ('This condition ensures that the model possesses OOD Detection'), cross-references are broken (referencing non-existent 'Table 4.2' and 'Table 4.3' instead of Tables 5 and 6), and macros are repeatedly misformatted ('Eq. equation 11-equation 13', 'scAtter plots').

strengths: The paper tackles an important and relevant problem: improving the out-of-distribution (OOD) detection capabilities of transformer backbones across both computer vision (ViT) and natural language processing (BERT).

The experimental section encompasses diverse settings, evaluating on multiple image benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200) as well as text classification tasks with semantic and background shifts (CLINC150, IMDB/Yelp).
weaknesses: Theoretical disconnect and limited utility: While Theorems 1 and 2 (Theorems 4 and 5 in the appendix) attempt to analyze PAC learnability and Jackson-type error bounds for transformers, there is a fundamental gap between this theory and the proposed GROD algorithm. The theorems rely on finite dataset assumptions ($|\mathcal{X}| < +\infty$) to guarantee learnability via universal approximation/memorization, which is a standard expressivity property. The theory does not explain or justify why PCA/LDA-based boundary synthesis or Mahalanobis filtering yields representative or optimal synthetic outliers.

Degenerate theoretical bounds: In Theorem 2 / Theorem 5, the lower bound on the learnability probability contains an exponent of $(K+1)n + 1$. Because this exponent scales linearly with the dataset size $n$, the theoretical lower bound rapidly decays to zero for any realistically sized dataset unless the error term is vanishingly small, significantly undermining the practical relevance of the bound.

Questionable and inconsistent empirical results: On CIFAR-10 (Table 2), GROD reports an AUROC of 99.98% and an FPR95 of 0.12% against near-OOD CIFAR-100 without using real outlier exposure. This near-zero error on a notoriously difficult near-OOD task raises questions about potential data leakage or evaluation discrepancies. Furthermore, this dramatic performance does not transfer when CIFAR-100 is used as ID (Table 3), where GROD achieves an AUROC of only 91.34% and is frequently matched or outperformed by standard baselines like VIM and CIDER.

Limited algorithmic originality: The core concept of synthesizing virtual outliers near class boundaries in latent feature space to train an auxiliary OOD head is already well-established by methods such as VOS and NPOS. Using linear projections (PCA/LDA) and Mahalanobis filtering represents an incremental heuristic variation of existing outlier synthesis pipelines.

Presentation flaws and unpolished text: The manuscript contains notable writing defects, including an incomplete sentence at the end of the abstract ('The code is available a'), incorrect table and equation cross-references (e.g., referring to 'Table 4.2' instead of Table 5, 'Table 4.3' instead of Table 6, and recurring 'Eq. equation' phrasing), and absent error bars or confidence intervals across runs.
